# The metamodel is generated by one compilation and consumed by another, in its own process

Queries and sorts in this project name entity properties through the generated `Category_`,
`Transaction_` and friends rather than through string literals, so that renaming a field breaks
the build instead of a request. Generating that metamodel with `hibernate-jpamodelgen` in the
same `javac` run that compiles the code reading it produces class files that are quietly wrong.

The damage is a constant pool entry that names a class without its package. `TransactionService`
ends up referring to `LCategoryRepository;` where it should say
`Lcom/igorpujovic/finance_tracker/category/CategoryRepository;`. Nothing reports it. `javac`
exits zero, the class file is the right size, and the build is green. The failure arrives at
class loading, as a `NoClassDefFoundError` naming a class that is sitting in `target/classes` —
in a test suite, as every `@SpringBootTest` in the module failing to build an application
context; in production, as an application that will not start. Which classes are hit varies from
run to run, and they are always the ones near the generated metamodel.

It is frequent, not a curiosity. Measured on this machine over eight clean builds of the step-2
tree, five were corrupt. The note on issue 02 blamed the incremental check and turned it off,
which was a real bug with a similar shape — a class silently missing rather than silently
wrong — but it was not this one, and this one survived the fix.

Two conditions each cause it, and both have to go. Annotation processing in the consuming
compilation is one: a compilation with no processing rounds, handed the generated sources as
ordinary files, was clean ten times out of ten where processing was corrupt five times out of
eight. Reuse of the in-process compiler is the other: splitting the build into a
processing-only pass and a processing-free pass left the second pass — the second `javac` in
that JVM — corrupt five times in twelve, always in the same class. So the metamodel is
generated by a `proc:only` compilation bound to `generate-sources`, the real compilation runs
with `proc:none` over the sources and the generated directory together, and `<fork>true</fork>`
gives each compilation a `javac` of its own. Together: no corruption in twenty-four clean
builds, against a baseline of five in eight.

The generated sources go to `target/generated-sources/metamodel` rather than the conventional
`generated-sources/annotations`, because each compiler execution clears its own generated
directory before it runs, and sharing one would have the second pass delete what the first
wrote. The second pass names its source roots explicitly for the same reason the first needs a
directory of its own: the directory is registered as a source root by the execution that
generates into it, and that is no longer the execution that compiles.

Rejected alternatives: pinning `maven-compiler-plugin` to 3.14.0 (identical failure rate),
`-XDuseUnsharedTable=false` (no effect once the compiler is reused), and forking alone, which
reduced it to one build in twelve rather than removing it. Committing the generated metamodel
to `src` was rejected because it would let a renamed field survive in a stale attribute, which
is the whole reason the metamodel is generated.

## Consequences

The build costs one extra compilation of the main sources and a `javac` process per execution:
`mvn clean test-compile` went from about 5.4 to about 7.2 seconds on this machine. In exchange a
green build means what it says.

Anyone simplifying this configuration back to one pass, or dropping `fork`, will get a build
that passes and an application that does not start, on roughly every other run. The two
executions and the fork are load-bearing, and the pom says so at each of them.

Both conditions are about `javac` and the processor rather than about this project, so a future
JDK or `hibernate-jpamodelgen` may fix the underlying defect and make this unnecessary. Whoever
tries that should measure it the way it was measured here: a dozen clean builds, checking the
compiled classes for unqualified names, because a single green build proves nothing.
